proxy_language: Old Javanese (Kawi), with Austronesian (Proto-Malayo-Polynesian) background; Old Balinese as secondary
proxy_rationale: The label combines wet-rice and volcanic court polities of Java/Bali (Mataram, Kediri, Majapahit, Bali) with Vietnam and Indonesia generally. Old Javanese is richly attested in inscriptions and kakawin literature (8th-15th c.) and is the best-documented court language of the region. Vietnamese court language (Chinese/Sino-Vietnamese plus Vietic) is a different family and is not covered here; the Vietnam component is therefore only loosely represented. Names also include Sanskrit-derived court vocabulary, which is authentic for Old Javanese courts.
phonology: Vowels: a, i, u, e (schwa, written e or e-acute), o, plus Sanskrit-derived long vowels (a-macron, i-macron, u-macron) and ai, au. Consonants: stops p b t d c j k g (with Sanskrit-derived aspirates kh gh th dh ph bh and retroflexes in learned words); nasals m n ng ny; fricatives s, h (plus learned sh); liquids r l; glides w y. Old Javanese distinguishes dental and retroflex series in inherited and Sanskrit-derived words (t/d vs. retroflex).
phonotactics: Native roots are mostly disyllabic, shapes (C)V(C)CV(C) with CVCVC and CVCCVC common. Final consonants allowed in native words: -k, -t, -p, -m, -n, -ng, -r, -l, -s, -h, -w, -y (final voiced stops devoice or are avoided in native roots). Clusters inside words are homorganic nasal+stop (mb, nd, nj, ngg are common spelling in Modern Javanese) or r/l/s + C; word-initial clusters occur mainly in Sanskrit loans (e.g. sri, prabu, kr-, tr-). Penultimate stress; schwa common in open penultimate syllables.
orthography: Scholarly Latin transliteration of Old Javanese/Kawi script (Zoetmulder convention): ng, ny, c, j, e for schwa (e-acute in some editions), diacritics for Sanskrit long vowels (a-macron etc.) and retroflexes (dotted letters) in learned terms. Modern-style romanisation also acceptable: c = ch, j = j, y = y, ng, ny; u not v; w not v.
morphology: Agglutinative with affixation: prefixes ma- (verb/stative), mang-/ang- (active verbal with nasal assimilation), pa-/pang- (agent/instrument/place nouns, e.g. pa-...-an place), ka-, sa- (one/all), tang-, a-; suffixes -an (place/result/collective), -a, -i, -ana (applicative), -ing / -ning (genitive/definite linker after vowel/consonant), -nya (3sg poss.). Infixes -um- (active), -in- (passive), -el-/-er- (plural/intensive, rare). Reduplication is productive (full or partial) for plural/intensity. No noun classes, case or tone. Titles and honorifics: sang, sri, mpu, rakai, dyah, haji, ratu, bhatara/bhatari.
compounding: Head-initial: modifier follows head. Genitive 'X of Y' is X + Y directly or with the linker -ning/-ing (X-ning Y), e.g. 'lord of the mountain' = sang hyang giri / prabu ning gunung. Agent/maker names use pa-/pang- prefix (pandai 'smith', pamangku, pangiwa) or tuha/mpu + noun (mpu gandring 'master of ...'). Place names use pa-...-an or Sanskrit -pura/-nagara/-dwipa/-giri/-wana compounds (Sanskrit compounds are head-final: Singasari, Dwipantara).
noun_phrase_order: Head noun + modifier (adjective, possessor, demonstrative follow): banyu wening 'clear water'; gunung agung 'great mountain'; wwang ika 'that person'. Numerals precede the noun (rwa wwang 'two people'). Titles precede the personal name (sang ..., sri ...).
sources: Zoetmulder, Kalangwan: A Survey of Old Javanese Literature (1974)
Uhlenbeck, A Critical Survey of Studies on the Languages of Java and Madura (1964)
Adelaar and Himmelmann (eds.), The Austronesian Languages of Asia and Madagascar (2005)
notes: Vietnamese court naming (Sino-Vietnamese, Vietic) is outside this proxy; if a Vietnam flavour is wanted, use a separate Sino-Vietnamese layer, not Old Javanese. Sanskrit loans (giri, surya, dewi, bhatara, nagara) are authentic court vocabulary. No word may be identical to a Modern Irish, Scottish Gaelic or Manx word unless the language is Goidelic.
